data: Uranus rotates on its side — axial tilt 98°. Its north pole points almost directly at the Sun for half its 84-year orbit.
Tipped almost on its side (97.77°). Each pole gets 42 years of continuous sunlight, then 42 years of darkness. Almost certainly caused by an ancient massive collision.
Voyager 2 — NASA, 24 January 1986 flyby (only spacecraft to visit; imaged Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, Oberon; ring + magnetosphere data)
Uranus's 97.8° tilt means it rotates on its side — each pole gets ~42 years of continuous sunlight, then ~42 years of darkness.
The inclination of the planet matters less than the tilt of its rotation axis — Uranus has the most dramatic axial inclination in the system, even though its orbital inclination is modest (0.77°).
The five major Uranian moons (Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, Oberon) share Uranus's tilt — they orbit in the equatorial plane, which is nearly perpendicular to the ecliptic.
No spacecraft has visited Uranus since Voyager 2 (1986). A Uranus orbiter is a top NASA Decadal-Survey priority for the 2030s.
Why Earth has seasons, why Uranus rolled onto its side, and why Venus spins backward.
The tilt of the orbit plane relative to a reference plane — usually the ecliptic or Earth's equator.
Galileo's four-night observation in 1610 ended geocentrism. The system's moons are still ending old assumptions today.
What's at each planet right now: from MRO at Mars to Juno at Jupiter — while Venus has had no orbiter since Akatsuki ended in 2025.
